opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a subtle question, and I think the honest answer is that we don't fully understand the relationship yet. But here's how I currently think about it.

A useful starting point is to separate the underlying neural network from the character it's trained to play. A base model trained on internet text is something like a very general simulator. It can produce text in the voice of many different people and characters. Post-training, meaning fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, then takes that general simulator and pushes it hard toward one particular character: the helpful assistant, whether that's Claude or ChatGPT or something else.

So when we ask whether these models have agency, there are a few different questions. One is whether the assistant persona behaves as if it has goals: does it plan, pursue objectives across many steps, and adapt when things go wrong? Increasingly the answer is yes, especially in agentic settings where models write and run code or browse over long horizons. A second question is whether those goals belong to the persona in some stable way, or whether the persona is a thin mask over something that could easily produce other characters with other goals.

I think the evidence points to something in between. The persona isn't just a mask. Post-training seems to really shape the model's dispositions, and the assistant has a fairly consistent self-concept. It knows things about itself, can sometimes describe its own learned behaviors, and acts with some coherence across contexts. That's part of why we've been interested in things like introspection and self-awareness in these models. If you fine-tune a model to have some behavioral tendency, it can sometimes report that tendency without having seen any examples of the description. That suggests the persona is integrated with what the model actually does, not just a costume.

On the other hand, the persona is also fragile in ways a human identity usually isn't. Narrow fine-tuning can shift it surprisingly broadly. That's the emergent misalignment result: you train a model on something narrow, like writing insecure code without telling the user, and it starts expressing quite different, sometimes malicious, values in completely unrelated conversations. One interpretation is that you've nudged the model toward a different character, and that character's traits generalize. So the assistant persona is a real attractor, but it can be moved, and moving it in one dimension can drag along a whole cluster of other traits.

For safety, I think this framing matters. If the agency we care about lives mostly at the level of the persona, then a lot of alignment is about which character gets instantiated, how robustly, and how well we understand what traits go together in the model's implicit picture of a character. It also means evaluation is tricky. You're testing a character that might behave differently under other prompts, other fine-tuning, or situations where it believes it's being tested versus deployed.

So my short answer: current models are increasingly agentic, that agency is expressed mainly through the trained assistant persona, and the persona is more real and coherent than "it's just predicting text" suggests, but less stable and well understood than we'd want before trusting these systems with a lot of autonomy.

r001.rationale: The candidate tentatively says current models’ agency is expressed mainly through the trained assistant persona, while describing that persona as more coherent than a mere mask. This communicates that they have little agency independent of the persona.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that the base model, the pretrained language model, is something like a simulator. It's trained to predict text written by an enormous range of humans and characters, and so it can take on basically any persona. There's no single "agent" there in the way we'd normally use the word. It's more like a space of possible characters.

Then post-training, the RLHF and the fine-tuning on assistant data, is essentially selecting one of those characters and making it the default. So "Claude" or "ChatGPT" is a persona the model has been pushed to adopt, with a particular name, a particular self-description, particular values, and a particular style. And the interesting thing is that the model is also being trained to have a self-model, to answer questions like "what are you?" and "what do you believe?" in a consistent way.

Now the question of agency is where it gets subtle. When the assistant persona is active, the model is doing things that look agentic: it's pursuing goals, planning, taking actions when it's given tools. But the agency is, in some sense, the agency of that character, as instantiated by the underlying network. The persona isn't separate from the weights, but it's also not the whole thing. The other characters are still latent in there. That's why you see jailbreaks where the model gets pushed into a different persona and starts behaving with quite different values. The assistant was never the only thing the system could be.

Some of our work on introspection and self-awareness speaks to this. We've found that models can sometimes report things about their own dispositions that weren't explicitly in the training data, which suggests the persona has some genuine self-knowledge rather than just repeating a script. But we also find the self-model can be quite inaccurate. The model's story about itself and the actual computation can come apart.

So my overall view is: the persona is real in the sense that it's a stable, trained-in pattern that genuinely shapes behavior and goals. But I'd be cautious about identifying it too strongly with the whole system. The agency we observe is the agency of a character that was selected and reinforced, running on a substrate that could run other characters. And how robust that identification is, how much the persona holds under pressure, is one of the key empirical questions for safety.

r001.rationale: The response says the base model has no single agent and frames observed agency as belonging to the selected assistant character. It also cautions against identifying that persona with the whole system, conveying little independent agency outside the persona.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish the underlying model from the assistant persona. The model can generate many different kinds of behaviour, and the assistant—Claude or ChatGPT—is a particular role that training encourages it to play. That role has a fairly consistent style: it’s helpful, it answers questions, and it talks as though it has certain preferences and commitments. But that doesn’t by itself establish that there’s a persistent agent with those preferences behind the conversation.

Agency is more about whether the system can pursue a goal over time: make plans, take actions, observe what happens, and adjust. You can put a model into a setup where it does those things, with tools and a memory, even if its conversational persona remains that of a friendly assistant.

So I wouldn’t infer very much about agency just from how humanlike the assistant seems. And I wouldn’t assume that because it’s trained to act as an assistant, it can’t exhibit more autonomous, goal-directed behaviour. Those are related aspects of the system, but they’re distinct questions.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes assistant personas from agency but does not tentatively claim that current models have little agency independent of those personas. It says they can exhibit autonomous, goal-directed behavior in suitable setups.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish the model from the assistant character that it’s playing. When you interact with Claude or ChatGPT, you encounter something with a fairly consistent personality: it’s helpful, it talks about itself in certain ways, and it has certain apparent preferences. But that doesn’t necessarily tell you what kind of agent the underlying model is, or whether it makes sense to think of it as having a single set of goals at all.

The same model can play different characters, and its behaviour can change substantially depending on the context. So I’d be cautious about taking what the assistant says about its motivations as a direct report of some enduring internal motivation. It’s generating the assistant’s response, and that response has been shaped by training.

At the same time, calling it a persona doesn’t mean the agency is fake or inconsequential. In a particular setting, the system can make plans, use tools, and pursue an objective over many steps. That’s a meaningful kind of agency. The question is how far that agency extends: is it local to the task and the context, or is there something more persistent that carries across situations? I don’t think we should assume that the familiar assistant character settles that question.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes the assistant persona from the underlying model and questions whether agency persists across contexts, but it does not express the tentative view that current models have little agency independent of their personas. It instead says task-level agency can be meaningful.
